title: Prompt Engineering
tagline: Get clear, reliable results from AI assistants, with hands-on practice in every module
summary: Learn to work with AI assistants effectively and responsibly: how language models behave, how to write structured prompts, techniques such as examples and step-by-step reasoning, how to test and improve prompts, and how to use AI safely for study and work. Every module has a hands-on lab. No coding is required, and the labs do not call any AI service.

modules.title: AI foundations
modules.summary: What language models are, what they can and cannot do and why prompts matter.
modules.outcome: You can explain in plain words how a language model works, describe its strengths and limits and say why wording changes the result.
modules.intro: AI assistants have become part of everyday study and work. To use them well you do not need to know how to build one, but you do need an accurate mental model of what they are doing, otherwise you will either over-trust them or ignore their best uses.

topics.title: How a language model works
topics.html:
Definition

Large language model (LLM). A computer program trained on very large amounts of text to predict what text is likely to come next. By repeating that prediction it can write, summarise, translate and answer questions.

The model does not look things up in a database of facts. Its knowledge is stored in patterns learned during training. That explains both its impressive fluency and its weak spots: it can produce a convincing sentence that happens to be false, because plausibility and truth are not the same thing.

Useful terms
TermMeaning
TokenA piece of text, often part of a word; about 0.75 of an English word on average
PromptThe input you give the model
Context windowHow much text the model can consider at once
Training dataThe text the model learned from, which has a cut-off date
HallucinationA confident but false or invented output
Tip

Think of an assistant as a very well-read colleague who sometimes bluffs. Ask for reasoning, give it your sources and check what matters.

Check what you just learned

1. A language model mainly:
  • Looks up a database of verified facts
  • Predicts likely text from patterns (correct)
  • Searches the live internet always
  • Reads your mind

Plausible text is not always true.
keyPoints: A language model predicts likely text from learned patterns.
Fluent does not mean true.

topics.title: Strengths and limits
topics.html:
Strong at
TaskWhy it works
Rewriting and editingLanguage transformation is its core skill
Summarising supplied textThe facts are in front of it
BrainstormingMany options are wanted, not one correct answer
Explaining at different levelsPatterns of explanation are common
Drafting structure and outlinesFamiliar forms
Translating and reformattingMapping between forms
Weak at, or risky for
TaskRisk
Exact facts, quotes, citationsMay invent details
Recent eventsTraining has a cut-off; no live data unless connected to tools
Precise calculationsUse a calculator or spreadsheet
Legal, medical or financial decisionsErrors can harm; consult a professional
Anything needing your private contextIt only knows what you tell it
Watch out

Do not use an AI answer as the final word on health, legal or money matters. Use it to prepare questions for a qualified person.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the riskiest use?
  • Rewriting your email
  • Brainstorming names
  • Listing legal citations from memory (correct)
  • Summarising text you pasted

Invented references occur.
keyPoints: Strong with language tasks on supplied text; risky for exact facts and citations.
Spend checking effort where mistakes cost most.

topics.title: Why prompts matter
topics.html:
The model can only respond to what you give it. A vague prompt leaves it to guess your audience, your goal and your standards, and it will fill those gaps with the most common assumptions. A clear prompt narrows the guess.

Worked example

Same request, different prompts

You need a short bio for a club website.

  1. Weak: Write a bio.
  2. Better: Write a 60-word third-person bio for the Photography Club of a school, friendly tone, mentioning weekly walks and a yearly exhibition.

Answer. The better prompt gives the audience, length, tone and facts.

What a good prompt supplies
IngredientQuestion it answers
TaskWhat do I want done?
ContextWhat does the model need to know?
Audience and toneWho is this for and how should it sound?
ConstraintsWhat are the limits: length, scope, things to avoid?
FormatHow should the answer be laid out?
ExamplesWhat does a good result look like?
Tip

If you would need to ask a human assistant three clarifying questions, answer them in the prompt.

Check what you just learned

1. A good prompt reduces:
  • The need for any checking
  • The need to read
  • The cost of the internet
  • Guesswork about your intent (correct)

Specifics narrow the possibilities.

Key terms: flip and sort

LLM
A large language model
Token
A piece of text processed by the model
Hallucination
A confident false output
Context window
How much text the model can consider
Prompt
The input given to the model
keyPoints: The model fills gaps with common assumptions; clear prompts narrow them.
Supply task, context, audience, constraints and format.

modules.title: Prompt basics
modules.summary: Write clear prompts with the right ingredients and learn to improve weak ones.
modules.outcome: You can structure a prompt with role, task, context, constraints and format, and rewrite vague requests into specific ones.
modules.intro: Most improvements in AI results come from simple clarity. This module gives you a repeatable structure so that you do not have to start from a blank page.

topics.title: A prompt template
topics.html:
Formula · A reusable structure

Role + Task + Context + Constraints + Format

Role: study coach. Task: make a timetable. Context: exam dates and weak subjects. Constraints: 4 hours a day. Format: a table.

Each part in detail
PartWhat to writeExample
RoleWho the assistant should act as (optional but useful)You are an experienced study coach.
TaskOne clear actionCreate a two-week revision timetable.
ContextRelevant factsExams on 12, 14, 17 and 19 March; weak in Physics.
ConstraintsLimits and preferencesAt most 4 hours a day; a day off on Sunday.
FormatHow to lay out the answerA table with date, subject, topic and hours.

You do not need all five every time. For a quick question, a clear task is enough. For anything important, the more of the structure you use, the fewer revisions you will need.

Tip

Put the most important instruction first and the material to work on at the end, clearly separated, for example between lines of three dashes.

Common mistakes

  • Packing several unrelated tasks into one prompt.
  • Leaving out the text you want the model to work on.
  • Using unclear words such as 'good' or 'short' without a number.
  • Forgetting to say who the answer is for.

Check what you just learned

1. The 'constraints' part states:
  • Limits and preferences (correct)
  • The role
  • The format only
  • Nothing

For example length or hours per day.
keyPoints: Role, task, context, constraints and format.
Use as much structure as the task deserves.

topics.title: Be specific
topics.html:
Vague to specific
VagueSpecific
Write something about climate.Explain how solar panels work to a 12-year-old in 150 words, with one everyday analogy.
Make my CV better.Here is my CV and a job advert. List three gaps and suggest one improvement for each, as bullet points.
Give me ideas.Give me ten names for a college coding club, each with a one-line reason.
Summarise this.Summarise this report in five bullet points for a busy manager; highlight any decisions needed.

Ways to add specificity

  1. Name the audience and their level.
  2. Give numbers: words, items, minutes.
  3. State the purpose: why do you need it?
  4. Say what to include and what to avoid.
  5. Provide the source text instead of asking from memory.

How much detail is enough?

Change the number of ingredients you include and watch the estimated clarity score. It is a rough teaching model, not a measurement of any real system.

Adjust Task is clear (0 or 1), Context given (0 or 1), Constraints given (0 or 1), Format given (0 or 1), Examples given (0 or 1) and see Clarity score out of 100 change.

Watch out

More words are not always better. Padding with irrelevant detail can distract the model. Add what changes the answer.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the most specific?
  • Write about dogs
  • Write 100 words about how to train a puppy to sit, for a first-time owner (correct)
  • Dogs
  • Tell me stuff

Audience, topic and length are given.
keyPoints: Add audience, numbers, purpose and the source text.
Detail should change the answer; avoid padding.

topics.title: Working with the answer
topics.html:
A conversation with an assistant is not one-shot. Your first prompt gets you a draft; follow-ups steer it. Treat the answer as raw material.

Follow-up moves
MoveExample
NarrowKeep only the three most important points.
ExpandAdd an example for the second point.
Change toneMake it friendlier and less formal.
Change formatTurn this into a table.
ChallengeWhat assumptions are you making? What might be wrong?
Ask for alternativesGive two different versions.
RestartStart fresh with this clearer prompt.

Habits

  • Say exactly what to change instead of 'make it better'.
  • Keep the good parts: 'keep paragraphs 1 and 3 as they are'.
  • If the conversation drifts, start a new one with a refined prompt.
  • Save prompts that work.
Tip

When an answer is wrong, point to the exact line and say what is wrong and what the correct fact is, rather than just asking it to try again.

Check what you just learned

1. A better follow-up than 'make it better' is:
  • Make it more
  • Do it again
  • Shorten paragraph two to 20 words and add an example (correct)
  • Fix it

Specific edits work.

Key terms: flip and sort

Role
The perspective the assistant takes
Constraint
A limit on the answer
Format
The layout of the answer
Follow-up
A message that refines the previous answer
Placeholder
A marked gap to fill in a reusable prompt
keyPoints: Treat the first answer as a draft and steer with specific follow-ups.
Restart with a better prompt if the conversation drifts.

modules.title: Prompting techniques
modules.summary: Use examples, step-by-step reasoning, roles and formats to get more reliable results.
modules.outcome: You can use few-shot examples, ask for reasoning, set roles and request structured formats.
modules.intro: Beyond clarity, a few patterns reliably improve results. They are tools, not magic words: each works because it supplies information the model would otherwise have to guess.

topics.title: Examples (few-shot prompting)
topics.html:
Showing is often clearer than telling. A few examples of input and desired output teach the pattern, tone and format at once.

Worked example

Labelling comments

Task: label comments as Positive, Neutral or Negative.

  1. Comment: Quick delivery and hot food. Label: Positive
  2. Comment: It arrived as described. Label: Neutral
  3. Comment: Nobody answered my calls for two hours. Label: Negative
  4. Comment: The app is easy but prices are high. Label:

Answer. The model continues the pattern.

Tips

  • Use two to five examples, varied enough to show the range.
  • Keep the format of the examples identical.
  • Include at least one tricky case.
  • Check that the examples themselves are correct, since the model will copy their mistakes.
  • Put the real input last, in the same form.
Zero, one and few-shot
TypeExamples givenWhen to use
Zero-shotNoneSimple, well-known tasks
One-shotOneShow a format
Few-shotSeveralCustom labels, tone or structure

Check what you just learned

1. Few-shot prompting uses:
  • No examples
  • A password
  • Only a role
  • Several examples (correct)

It shows the pattern.
keyPoints: Examples teach pattern, tone and format.
Keep examples consistent and correct.

topics.title: Reasoning step by step
topics.html:
For problems with several steps, asking the model to work through the steps often improves accuracy and lets you check the logic. Writing out the reasoning gives the model room to avoid shortcuts and gives you something to verify.

Ways to request reasoning
PromptEffect
Work through this step by step before answering.Shows the chain of thought
List your assumptions first.Exposes hidden premises
Give your answer, then explain how you checked it.Adds a verification step
Solve it two different ways and compare.Catches inconsistencies
Worked example

A word problem

A train travels 180 km in 3 hours, then 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

  1. Step 1: total distance = 180 + 120 = 300 km.
  2. Step 2: total time = 3 + 2 = 5 hours.
  3. Step 3: average speed = 300 / 5 = 60 km/h.

Answer. Seeing the steps lets you spot a wrong one.

Watch out

Visible reasoning can sound convincing even when wrong. Check key numbers and steps yourself, especially for maths, logic and anything important.

Check what you just learned

1. Why ask for step-by-step reasoning?
  • It makes errors easier to find and often improves accuracy (correct)
  • It always guarantees correctness
  • It reduces tokens
  • It hides mistakes

Visible steps help checking.
keyPoints: Ask for steps, assumptions and checks.
Verify the reasoning; it can be wrong.

topics.title: Roles, formats and delimiters
topics.html:
Setting a role
RoleEffect
You are a patient maths tutor for Class 9.Simpler language and worked steps
You are a sceptical editor.More critical feedback
You are a hiring manager reviewing a CV.Employer's perspective

Roles guide tone and depth. They do not give the model new knowledge or authority; 'you are a doctor' does not make its medical advice reliable.

Common output formats
FormatPrompt snippetGood for
BulletsAnswer in five bullet pointsQuick reading
TableReturn a table with columns A, B and CComparison
StepsGive numbered stepsProcedures
JSONReturn valid JSON with keys name and summaryUse by programs
Word limitNo more than 100 wordsControl length

Using delimiters

  • Separate instructions from material with markers such as triple dashes or quotation marks.
  • Label the material: 'Text to summarise: ...'.
  • State clearly where the material ends.
  • This prevents the model from confusing your text with instructions.

Check what you just learned

1. A role like 'you are a doctor' makes the answer:
  • Medically reliable
  • Phrased with a doctor's tone, but still unverified (correct)
  • Legally binding
  • Always true

Do not mistake style for expertise.

Key terms: flip and sort

Few-shot
Giving several examples in the prompt
Zero-shot
Giving no examples
Chain of thought
Step-by-step reasoning
Delimiter
A marker that separates parts of a prompt
Structured output
An answer in a defined format
keyPoints: Roles shape tone, not authority.
Request formats explicitly and separate instructions from material.

modules.title: Evaluating and improving prompts
modules.summary: Test prompts on several inputs, score the results and improve them step by step.
modules.outcome: You can create a small test set, score outputs with a rubric, compare prompt versions and estimate costs.
modules.intro: One good answer proves little. A prompt that will be used repeatedly deserves a quick test on a few different inputs, just as a recipe is tried more than once.

topics.title: Test sets and rubrics
topics.html:
A rubric example for a summary
Criterion1 (poor)3 (fair)5 (excellent)
AccuracyHas errorsMinor slipsAll facts correct
CompletenessMisses key pointsMost pointsAll key points
BrevityRamblingA little longRight length
ClarityConfusingMostly clearVery clear

Keep the rubric short and write it before you look at results, so you do not adjust the standard to fit the answers.

Rules

  • Change one thing at a time, so you know what helped.
  • Include inputs that are edge cases: very short, very long, odd formats.
  • Keep a record of versions and scores.
  • Remember that outputs vary between runs; try each input a couple of times.
Tip

The worst output matters as much as the average. A prompt that is usually great but occasionally disastrous may not be fit for use.

Check what you just learned

1. Why change one thing at a time?
  • To save time
  • It is required
  • To know what caused the change (correct)
  • To cost less

Otherwise causes are mixed.
keyPoints: Test on several inputs, score with a rubric, change one thing at a time.
Look at the worst case as well as the average.

topics.title: Common failures and fixes
topics.html:
Problem and remedy
ProblemLikely causeTry
Too long or too shortNo length constraintState a number of words or sentences
Wrong toneNo audience or roleName the audience and tone
Invented factsAsked from memoryProvide the source and say 'use only this text'
Ignores part of the instructionToo many tasks at onceSplit into steps or numbered requirements
Inconsistent formatNo example or format givenShow an example of the exact format
Generic answerToo little contextAdd specifics, examples and constraints
Worked example

Reducing invention

Instead of 'Tell me about the causes of the 1857 uprising', give the textbook passage and say: 'Using only the text below, list the causes. If the text does not say, write Not stated.'

  1. The answer is limited to your source.
  2. A refusal option reduces made-up details.

Answer. Grounding the model in supplied text reduces hallucination.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a good answer once means it always works.
  • Adding more and more instructions until they conflict.
  • Believing specific numbers and quotes without checking.

Check what you just learned

1. To reduce invented facts you should:
  • Ask for longer answers
  • Use capitals
  • Add a role
  • Give the source text and limit the answer to it (correct)

Grounding helps.
keyPoints: Match each failure to a fix: constraints, sources, splitting, examples.
Grounding in supplied text reduces invention.

topics.title: Cost, length and speed
topics.html:
Many AI services charge by the amount of text processed, counted in tokens, for both your prompt and the answer. If you use an assistant through a paid interface for many requests, tokens become a budget item.

Formula · Token cost estimate

tokens ≈ words × 1.3; cost = tokens / 1000 × price per 1000 tokens

650 tokens per request × 2,000 requests = 1.3 million tokens. At an illustrative 2 rupees per 1,000 tokens that is about 2,600 rupees.

Estimate a monthly cost

Change the sizes and volume. The price is illustrative; always check the real price list of the service you use.

Adjust Prompt words, Answer words, Requests per month, Price per 1,000 tokens (rupees) and see Tokens per request, Monthly cost change.

Ways to control cost and time

  • Send only the text that matters.
  • Set a maximum length for answers.
  • Use smaller or cheaper models for simple tasks, where the service offers a choice.
  • Reuse good prompts rather than experimenting on large inputs.
  • Cache or save results you will need again.

Check what you just learned

1. Tokens in a prompt are:
  • Often what you are charged for, with the answer (correct)
  • Free always
  • Not counted
  • Only for images

Check the service's pricing.

Key terms: flip and sort

Rubric
A set of criteria for scoring
Test set
Inputs used to evaluate a prompt
Grounding
Basing the answer on supplied text
Iteration
Repeating with improvements
Edge case
An unusual input
keyPoints: Cost depends on tokens in and out.
Send only what matters and cap answer length.

modules.title: Safe and responsible use
modules.summary: Protect private information, respect honesty rules and recognise bias and misuse.
modules.outcome: You can decide what not to paste, check AI output before relying on it, disclose AI use appropriately and spot bias.
modules.intro: Powerful tools bring responsibilities. Using AI well includes protecting people's information, staying honest about your own work and being aware of the tool's blind spots.

topics.title: Privacy and confidentiality
topics.html:
Treat whatever you type into an online assistant as information you are sharing with a company. Providers differ in how they store and use it. Unless your school or employer has approved a tool for sensitive information, do not enter it.

What to keep out of prompts
CategoryExamples
SecretsPasswords, one-time codes, private keys
Identity dataID numbers, passport details, medical records
Other people's dataNames with marks, phone numbers, addresses
Business-confidential informationUnreleased plans, client lists, source code you are not allowed to share

Safer habits

  1. Remove or replace names and identifiers before pasting.
  2. Use dummy data when testing prompts.
  3. Check the service's privacy settings and your organisation's policy.
  4. Prefer tools approved by your organisation for work data.
Watch out

Never paste another person's private information into a public AI tool without a good reason and permission. Once shared, you cannot fully control where it goes.

Check what you just learned

1. Before pasting a document with customer names you should:
  • Paste it as is
  • Remove or replace the names and check the policy (correct)
  • Post it publicly
  • Add emojis

Protect personal data.
keyPoints: Do not enter secrets or other people's personal data into public tools.
Replace identifiers with placeholders.

topics.title: Honesty, learning and acknowledgement
topics.html:
Rules about AI vary: some courses and workplaces welcome it, some restrict it, and some require you to say when you have used it. The principle is the same everywhere: be honest about what is yours.

Healthy and unhealthy uses in study
HealthyUnhealthy
Asking for an explanation of a hard ideaSubmitting an AI-written essay as your own when this is not allowed
Getting feedback on your draftCopying answers in an exam
Making practice questionsLetting it do all thinking so you do not learn
Brainstorming then writing in your own wordsCiting sources you never read

Good practice

  • Read your institution's rules and follow them.
  • Use AI to learn, not to avoid learning.
  • Disclose AI help where required or where it matters.
  • Check facts and sources yourself.
  • Keep your own drafts and notes as evidence of your work.
Tip

Ask: would I be comfortable explaining exactly how I used the tool to my teacher or manager? If not, change what you are doing.

Check what you just learned

1. A healthy use of AI for study is:
  • Submitting its essay as yours where banned
  • Copying exam answers
  • Asking for an explanation then writing in your own words (correct)
  • Citing unread sources

It supports learning.
keyPoints: Follow the rules where you study or work.
Use AI to deepen learning, not to skip it.

topics.title: Bias, fairness and misuse
topics.html:
Models learn from human-written text, which contains stereotypes and gaps. As a result, they may produce biased or unbalanced content, or work better in some languages and cultures than others.

What to do

  • Notice and question stereotypes in outputs.
  • Ask for diverse perspectives or alternative viewpoints.
  • Be careful when using AI for decisions that affect people, such as hiring or grading.
  • Keep a human responsible for important decisions.
  • Report harmful outputs to the provider.
Misuse to avoid
MisuseWhy it matters
Creating deceptive content such as fake reviews or impersonationIt harms people and breaks rules and laws
Generating abuse or harassmentHarmful and unacceptable
Pretending machine-generated text is a person's testimonyDishonest
Relying on AI to make high-stakes decisions without reviewErrors can hurt people
Watch out

Deepfakes and synthetic images or voices can be used to deceive. Verify surprising media through trusted sources before sharing, and never create such content to deceive others.

Check what you just learned

1. For an important decision about a person you should:
  • Let AI decide alone
  • Hide the use of AI
  • Ignore bias
  • Keep a human responsible and review (correct)

Accountability must stay with people.

Key terms: flip and sort

Confidential
Private information not to be shared
Bias
A systematic unfairness or imbalance
Disclosure
Saying when AI was used
Deepfake
A synthetic media item made to look real
Accountability
Being responsible for a decision
keyPoints: Question bias; keep humans accountable for important decisions.
Do not use AI to deceive or harm.

modules.title: AI at work and study
modules.summary: Use assistants for writing, learning, analysis and automation, and build a personal prompt library.
modules.outcome: You can apply prompting to writing, studying, data tasks and everyday work, and keep a small library of reusable prompts.
modules.intro: This final module applies the skills to real tasks and shows how to build a reusable toolkit.

topics.title: Writing and communication
topics.html:
Useful writing prompts
TaskPrompt idea
Edit for clarityMake this paragraph clearer and shorter without changing the meaning. Show a list of what you changed.
Change toneRewrite this email to be polite but firm, under 100 words.
DraftDraft a one-page proposal outline for [project], with headings only.
ProofreadList spelling and grammar errors in this text, with corrections, but do not rewrite it.
SummariseSummarise this report for a busy manager in five bullets, then list any decisions needed.

In all these tasks, you supply the facts and the judgement; the assistant helps with wording and structure. Read the result as an editor would, and make sure the final text is true and sounds like you.

Common mistakes

  • Sending an AI draft without reading it.
  • Letting it invent facts to fill gaps.
  • Sounding generic: add your own details and voice.

Check what you just learned

1. Who is responsible for a message you send?
  • You (correct)
  • The AI
  • The provider
  • Nobody

You are accountable.
keyPoints: Use AI for editing, drafting and summarising; you own the facts and voice.
Always read before sending.

topics.title: Learning and analysis
topics.html:
Study uses

  • Ask for an explanation at your level, then ask for an example.
  • Ask it to quiz you on your notes, one question at a time.
  • Ask for a worked example, then try a similar problem yourself.
  • Ask it to find gaps in your summary of a topic.
  • Ask for a plan, then adapt it to your life.
A tutoring prompt
PartExample
RoleYou are a patient tutor.
TaskTeach me how to factorise quadratics.
MethodAsk me one question at a time and wait for my answer.
FeedbackTell me what I got right, then explain mistakes.
LimitDo not give the final answer until I try.

For data and analysis tasks, use AI to suggest approaches and formulas, but run the calculations in a spreadsheet or code you can check. Treat numbers from a chat answer as unverified until reproduced.

Tip

Teaching back is powerful: explain a topic to the assistant and ask it to find mistakes or gaps in your explanation.

Check what you just learned

1. A good tutoring prompt asks the assistant to:
  • Give all answers at once
  • Ask questions one at a time and wait (correct)
  • Avoid explanation
  • Write the exam

Active practice helps learning.
keyPoints: Use AI as a tutor, quiz-maker and gap-finder.
Reproduce numbers in a spreadsheet before trusting them.

topics.title: Your prompt library and habits
topics.html:
What to store with each prompt
FieldWhy
Name and purposeFind it later
Prompt with [placeholders]Reuse
Example input and outputRecall what good looks like
How I check itRemember what to verify
Date and versionTrack improvements

Habits of effective users

  • Give clear context every time.
  • Keep a human in the loop for important work.
  • Verify facts, numbers and sources.
  • Protect private information.
  • Stay curious: tools change quickly, but the habits of clarity and checking last.

Tools will keep changing. The prompts that work today may need adjustment next year. The durable skills are clear thinking, clear writing, careful checking and honesty about what you did.

Check what you just learned

1. Why store how you check each prompt?
  • For fun
  • To increase cost
  • To remember what to verify (correct)
  • To hide errors

Reliable habits matter.

Key terms: flip and sort

Prompt library
A collection of reusable prompts
Human in the loop
A person reviews important output
Placeholder
A marked space to fill in
Workflow
A repeatable way of doing a task
keyPoints: Store reusable prompts with placeholders and checks.
Clarity, checking and honesty outlast any tool.
